questions.q: A team proposes rewriting a slow service in a "faster" technology. How do you decide between optimising, re-architecting and rewriting?
questions.a:
### First, find where time goes
Most "slow service" problems are I/O patterns (N+1, chatty calls, missing indexes, sync blocking), data design, or configuration, not language speed. Profile and trace before deciding.

### Options
| Option | When | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| **Optimise in place** | hot spots identifiable and fixable (queries, caching, allocations) | low; incremental |
| **Re-architect parts** | structural issues: synchronous chains, hot rows, wrong data model, batch windows | medium; strangler approach |
| **Rewrite** | technology truly cannot meet requirements (for example microsecond latency, unsupported runtime), or codebase is unmaintainable and requirements changed fundamentally | high: second-system effect, lost edge-case knowledge, long time without value |

### Decision criteria
- Measured gap between current and required performance, and what each option achieves (prototype or benchmark the critical path).
- Cost and time to value; risk of regressions in correctness (financial logic).
- Team skills and operability of the new technology.
- Can you get 80% of the benefit with 20% of the effort by fixing the top bottlenecks?

### If rewriting
Strangle incrementally behind the same API, run shadow comparisons, migrate by cohort, keep the old system until parity is proven.
questions.code:
~~~yaml
# ADR-090: Pricing service performance (decision record)
status: accepted
context:
  requirement: p99 quote latency < 50 ms at 3k rps (currently 420 ms)
  proposal: rewrite in Go
analysis:
  traces: 78 percent of p99 is three sequential SQL lookups and one HTTP call to reference-data
  cpu_profile: JSON serialisation 12 percent, pricing math 6 percent
  prototype: in-memory rate snapshot + batched reference data cache in .NET -> p99 31 ms at 3.5k rps
decision: optimise in place (in-memory snapshots, caching, source-generated JSON); no rewrite
consequences:
  - 3 weeks of work instead of an estimated 6 months
  - revisit if requirement moves to sub-millisecond (would need different architecture, not just language)
~~~
pts: Profile and trace before deciding.
Most slowness is I/O and data design, not language.
Optimise, re-architect parts, or rewrite.
Prototype the critical path for each option.
If rewriting: strangle, shadow, migrate by cohort.
questions.ex: A proposed 6-month rewrite of a pricing service in another language was replaced by a 3-week optimisation after traces showed 78% of latency was sequential database lookups; a .NET prototype with in-memory snapshots beat the target.
fu: How do you prototype fairly?
When is a rewrite justified?
How do you preserve edge-case behaviour?

questions.q: You must choose between two databases (or message brokers) partly on performance. How do you run a fair, decision-grade benchmark?
questions.a:
### Define the decision
Workload profile from production: operations mix (reads, writes, scans), data volume and distribution (hot keys, tenant skew), concurrency, latency targets (p99), durability and consistency settings required, failure scenarios, cost envelope.

### Fairness rules
- **Same durability guarantees** (fsync, replication acks, isolation levels): comparing an async-acknowledged system with a synchronously replicated one is meaningless.
- Equivalent hardware and cost.
- Tuned by people who know each system (vendor input with your workload, not vendor benchmarks).
- Warm-up, steady state and long runs (compaction, GC, checkpoint effects show after hours).
- Measure with an open-model load generator; record full latency histograms.
- Include **failure behaviour**: node loss, network partition, failover time, recovery throughput.
- Operational tasks under load: backups, schema changes, scaling.

### Report
Throughput at target latency (not max throughput at any latency), latency curves vs load, behaviour at saturation, cost per unit of work, operational findings, and what was not tested.
questions.code:
~~~yaml
# Benchmark plan for ledger store selection
workload:
  source: production traces (Sep 2026), scaled 3x
  mix: { append_entry: 70, read_account_recent: 25, range_scan_statement: 5 }
  data: { accounts: 20M, entries: 4B, hot_accounts_pct: 0.5, hot_accounts_share_of_writes: 30 }
  concurrency: open model, 15k ops/s target, ramp to saturation
guarantees:
  durability: synchronous replication to 2 of 3 replicas, fsync on commit
  isolation: read committed snapshot; per-account ordering
environment: same instance types and storage (3 x 16 vCPU, 64 GB, premium SSD v2), same region
duration: { warmup: 30m, steady: 6h, soak: 24h }
failure_tests: [kill primary, network partition 60s, disk latency injection]
metrics: [p50, p99, p99.9 at 15k ops/s, max ops/s with p99 < 20ms, failover seconds, cost per million ops]
reviewers: [db-platform, ledger team, vendor SE for each product]
~~~
pts: Use your production workload profile.
Equal durability and consistency guarantees.
Equivalent hardware and cost; expert tuning.
Long runs, open-model load, full histograms.
Test failures and operations, not just throughput.
questions.ex: A vendor benchmark showed database A 5x faster than B; rerunning with synchronous replication on both and the bank's skewed account distribution showed A only 1.3x faster at p99 but with 4x longer failover. The decision went to B.
fu: How do you include cost fairly?
How long is long enough?
How do you avoid benchmarketing?

questions.q: Customers in Asia experience 800 ms extra latency on a Europe-hosted banking API. What are your options, considering data residency and consistency?
questions.a:
### Where latency comes from
Round trips over long distance (Asia to Europe RTT about 200 to 250 ms), multiplied by handshakes (TCP, TLS) and sequential calls; chatty APIs make it worse.

### Options (cheapest first)
| Option | Effect | Constraint |
|---|---|---|
| **Edge termination** (CDN or global accelerator near users) | TCP and TLS handshakes terminate nearby; persistent backbone connections | data still processed in Europe |
| Reduce round trips | aggregate APIs, HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, fewer sequential calls | client changes |
| **Edge caching** of public and reference content | no trip to origin | only cacheable data |
| **Regional read replicas or caches** for non-sensitive or permitted data | local reads | residency rules for personal data |
| **Regional deployment** (active-active or home region per customer) | full local processing | data residency (customer data home), consistency for global entities, cost |
| Async UX (optimistic UI, background sync) | perceived latency | correctness for money flows |

### Residency and consistency
Customer data often must stay in a jurisdiction; a home-region model (customers served by their home region, globally routed) respects it. Global entities (FX rates, reference data) replicate everywhere. Money movement across regions uses explicit cross-region processes, not distributed transactions.
pts: Distance times round trips drives latency.
Edge termination and fewer round trips first.
Edge caching for public and reference data.
Regional deployment with home-region data for residency.
Cross-region money flows as explicit processes.
questions.ex: An Asia-Pacific corporate client saw 1.2-second dashboard loads from a Europe-hosted API. Edge TLS termination, an aggregated dashboard endpoint and edge-cached reference data brought it to 450 ms without moving any customer data out of the EU.
fu: What does a global accelerator change?
How do you route by home region?
What consistency do global entities need?
pit: Replicating customer data without residency review.

questions.q: The transactions table grows by 2 billion rows a year. Plan for performance over the next five years: partitioning, archival, indexing and query design.
questions.a:
### Principles
Keep the **hot working set small**: most queries touch recent data (last 90 days to 13 months); old data is for statements, audits and analytics.

### Techniques
| Technique | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Table partitioning** by date (monthly) | partition elimination for date-bounded queries; fast archival via partition switch; per-partition index maintenance |
| Aligned indexes with the partition key plus the main access keys (account, date) | efficient seeks within partitions |
| **Archival tiers** | move partitions older than N months to cheaper storage (separate database, columnstore, data lake Parquet) with an access path for statements and audits |
| **Columnstore** for analytical history | compression (10x) and fast aggregates |
| Queries always bounded by date | partition elimination; no unbounded scans |
| Summary tables (monthly balances, totals) | avoid scanning history for common questions |
| Retention policy agreed with compliance | delete what you don't need to keep |

### Operations
Statistics and index maintenance per partition, automated partition creation ahead of time, monitoring of partition sizes, tested restore of archived data.

### Application
APIs default to recent windows; historical queries via async export jobs; read models for statements.
pts: Keep the hot working set small.
Monthly partitioning with aligned indexes.
Archive old partitions by switching; columnstore or lake.
Always date-bounded queries; summary tables.
Retention agreed with compliance; automated maintenance.
questions.ex: A 9-billion-row transactions table made index rebuilds take 30 hours and statement queries degrade. Monthly partitioning with partition switching to a columnstore archive kept the hot table at 18 months of data, and statement p99 returned to 40 ms.
fu: What if queries don't include the partition key?
How do you handle late-arriving back-dated transactions?
Columnstore vs data lake for history?
pit: Unbounded history in one hot table.

questions.q: Identify the performance anti-patterns typical of microservice architectures and how you fix them at the architecture level.
questions.a:
| Anti-pattern | Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| **Chatty synchronous chains** | p99 equals sum of many hops; cascading failures | aggregate APIs, data replication via events, async workflows |
| **Distributed monolith** | services always deployed and called together | merge services or redraw boundaries around business capabilities |
| **Entity services** (CRUD per table) | every use case calls 6 services | capability-oriented services owning their data |
| **Shared database** | lock contention and schema coupling across services | data ownership per service, events for sharing |
| **Fan-out without limits** | tail latency, connection exhaustion | batching, bounded parallelism, caches |
| **Retry storms** | overload after partial failures | retry budgets, one retry layer, circuit breakers |
| **Over-serialisation** | CPU spent on JSON between internal services | gRPC or binary formats, fewer hops |
| **Too many proxies** | gateway, mesh sidecars, ingress on every hop | trim layers; ambient mesh; direct paths for hot routes |
| **N+1 across services** | per-item remote calls | batch endpoints, local read models |
| **Synchronous cross-region calls** | 100+ ms per hop | regional ownership, async replication |

### Approach
Trace the critical journeys and count hops and calls per request; set budgets (max sequential hops); prioritise boundary changes where the same services always appear together.
questions.code:
~~~promql
# Hops per request for a journey: average number of client spans per server request at the BFF entry
sum(rate(traces_spanmetrics_calls_total{span_kind="SPAN_KIND_CLIENT", journey="view-statement"}[1h]))
/ sum(rate(traces_spanmetrics_calls_total{span_kind="SPAN_KIND_SERVER", service="mobile-bff", journey="view-statement"}[1h]))

# Services always called together (co-occurrence) suggests a distributed monolith: analyse service graph edges per trace offline
~~~
pts: Chatty sync chains and distributed monoliths.
Entity services and shared databases.
Unbounded fan-out and retry storms.
Too many proxies and over-serialisation.
Count hops per journey; redraw boundaries.
questions.ex: A "view statement" journey crossed 11 services with 38 calls per request; most were entity services fetching one table each. Consolidating into a statements capability with a local read model fed by events cut the journey to 3 hops and p99 from 2.4 s to 300 ms.
fu: How do you detect a distributed monolith?
When merge services?
How many hops are acceptable?

questions.q: An event-driven payment pipeline (initiation, fraud, ledger, notification) has variable end-to-end latency from 200 ms to 3 minutes. How do you analyse and improve it?
questions.a:
### Decompose end-to-end latency
For each stage: **queue time** (produce to consume), **processing time**, and **commit or publish delay** (outbox relay interval). End to end = sum along the slowest path.

### Typical causes of variability
| Cause | Fix |
|---|---|
| polling outbox relay with long intervals | CDC or shorter, adaptive polling |
| consumer lag at peaks | scale consumers up to partition count; more partitions planned ahead |
| hot partitions (one big merchant) | better keys (finer grain), dedicated handling |
| consumer batching waiting to fill | bound batches by time |
| retries with long backoff inside the main consumer | separate retry topics so healthy messages aren't blocked |
| rebalances during deploys | cooperative rebalancing, static membership |
| slow downstream in a stage | bulkheads, async calls, caching |
| GC pauses in consumers | allocation reduction |

### Measure
Producer timestamp in headers, per-stage queue latency histograms, business-level end-to-end SLO ("payment posted to ledger within 5 s, 99%"), traces linking stages.

### Improve
Fix the dominant stage first; set per-stage budgets; capacity-plan partitions and consumers for peaks.
questions.dia:
flowchart LR
  A[Initiation] -->|outbox relay delay| K1[[payments.initiated]]
  K1 -->|queue time| F[Fraud consumer]
  F -->|processing| K2[[payments.screened]]
  K2 -->|queue time| L[Ledger consumer]
  L --> K3[[payments.posted]]
  K3 --> N[Notifications]
  L -.retry topic.-> RT[[payments.screened.retry]]
pts: Decompose into queue, processing and publish delays.
Outbox relay intervals, lag, hot partitions, retries cause variance.
Separate retry topics; bounded batching.
Per-stage histograms and an end-to-end SLO.
Fix the dominant stage; plan partitions for peaks.
questions.ex: End-to-end posting latency spiked to minutes because a fraud consumer retried failed provider calls inline with 30-second backoff, blocking its partition. Moving retries to a retry topic and switching the outbox relay to CDC brought p99 from 3 minutes to 2.1 seconds.
fu: How do you size partition counts?
What is static group membership?
How do you handle ordering with retry topics?

questions.q: How do you communicate performance trade-offs and investment needs to product and business leaders who don't speak in percentiles?
questions.a:
### Translate to business outcomes
- Latency to **conversion and abandonment** (measured: each extra second on payment confirmation reduced completion by X%).
- Availability under peak to **revenue at risk** (transactions per minute times value times minutes of degradation).
- Cost per transaction and how it scales with growth.
- Customer complaints and NPS tied to slow journeys.
- Regulatory and SLA commitments (partner contracts with penalties).

### Present options, not demands
| Option | Cost | Outcome | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| do nothing | 0 | p99 doubles at forecast growth; peak failure probability high | revenue at risk on salary day |
| targeted fixes (caching, indexes) | 3 weeks | handles 2x growth | re-architecture needed next year |
| architecture change (partitioning) | 3 months | handles 10x | delivery risk, team focus |

### Make it visible
Journey dashboards with business metrics side by side with latency; post-incident reviews quantifying impact; performance budgets agreed with product as part of feature definitions ("this feature must not add more than 50 ms to checkout").

### Language
Plain words ("1 in 100 customers waits more than 3 seconds"), concrete scenarios, ranges with confidence, and trade-offs framed as choices the business owns.
questions.code:
~~~sql
-- Evidence for the conversation: payment completion rate by confirmation latency band (last 30 days)
SELECT CASE WHEN confirm_ms < 1000 THEN '<1s' WHEN confirm_ms < 2000 THEN '1-2s' WHEN confirm_ms < 4000 THEN '2-4s' ELSE '>4s' END AS latency_band,
       COUNT(*) AS attempts,
       AVG(CASE WHEN completed = 1 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END) AS completion_rate
FROM analytics.payment_attempts
WHERE started_at >= DATEADD(day, -30, GETUTCDATE())
GROUP BY CASE WHEN confirm_ms < 1000 THEN '<1s' WHEN confirm_ms < 2000 THEN '1-2s' WHEN confirm_ms < 4000 THEN '2-4s' ELSE '>4s' END
ORDER BY MIN(confirm_ms);
~~~
pts: Translate latency into conversion, revenue at risk, cost.
Present options with costs, outcomes and risks.
Show business metrics next to latency.
Agree performance budgets in feature definitions.
Plain language and ranges.
questions.ex: Engineering's request for a "performance sprint" was declined twice. Showing that payments confirmed in over 4 seconds completed 9 points less often, worth an estimated 1.2M a year, won funding for a targeted fix in the next planning cycle.
fu: How do you measure conversion impact causally?
How do you handle a product owner who wants features first?
How do you present uncertainty?

questions.q: The primary database is at 85% CPU at peak and growing. Walk through the decision between tuning, scaling up, read scaling, caching, partitioning and changing the data store.
questions.a:
### Step 1: understand the load
Query Store top consumers by CPU and reads, wait stats, read/write ratio, hot tables and rows, lock waits, growth trend. Often 10 queries are 70% of load.

### Step 2: options in order of effort
| Option | When it fits | Limits |
|---|---|---|
| **Tune** (indexes, query rewrites, plan fixes, fewer round trips) | top queries are inefficient | diminishing returns |
| **Scale up** (bigger tier, faster storage) | quick relief, buys time | cost grows non-linearly; a ceiling exists |
| **Read offload** (replicas, caches, read models, search) | read-heavy, staleness tolerable | consistency for decisions |
| **Write reduction** (batching, append-only patterns, removing hot rows) | write contention | design changes |
| **Partition / shard** by tenant or account | sustained write growth beyond one node | cross-shard queries, rebalancing, operations |
| **Different data store** for specific workloads (time series, search, key-value) | workload mismatched to relational engine | new operational surface |

### Decide
Model headroom per option against the growth forecast (months gained), cost, risk and team capacity. Typical sequence: tune now (weeks), scale up for headroom (days), offload reads (weeks), plan partitioning if growth demands (quarters).
questions.code:
~~~sql
-- Top CPU consumers in the last 7 days (Query Store): where tuning pays off first
SELECT TOP 15 q.query_id, LEFT(qt.query_sql_text, 120) AS query_text,
       SUM(rs.count_executions) AS executions,
       SUM(rs.avg_cpu_time * rs.count_executions) / 1e6 AS total_cpu_s,
       SUM(rs.avg_logical_io_reads * rs.count_executions) AS total_reads
FROM sys.query_store_query q
JOIN sys.query_store_query_text qt ON qt.query_text_id = q.query_text_id
JOIN sys.query_store_plan p ON p.query_id = q.query_id
JOIN sys.query_store_runtime_stats rs ON rs.plan_id = p.plan_id
JOIN sys.query_store_runtime_stats_interval i ON i.runtime_stats_interval_id = rs.runtime_stats_interval_id
WHERE i.start_time >= DATEADD(day, -7, SYSUTCDATETIME())
GROUP BY q.query_id, qt.query_sql_text
ORDER BY total_cpu_s DESC;
~~~
pts: Understand load: top queries, waits, ratios, hot rows.
Tune first; scale up for quick headroom.
Offload reads; reduce writes.
Partition or shard for sustained write growth.
Model months of headroom per option.
questions.ex: At 85% CPU, the top 8 queries accounted for 74% of load; tuning them dropped peak CPU to 45% in two weeks. Scaling up was then unnecessary for a year, and partitioning was planned calmly for the following year's growth.
fu: When is sharding unavoidable?
What about Azure SQL Hyperscale?
How do you shard a ledger?
pit: Scaling up repeatedly instead of tuning.

questions.q: Review the performance design of a new service before build. What is on your checklist, and what would you insist on before go-live?
questions.a:
| Area | Check | Insist before go-live |
|---|---|---|
| Requirements | journey SLOs (p99), peak forecast, growth | agreed budgets per hop |
| Critical path | sequential hops, fan-out, cross-region calls | hop count within budget |
| Data access | query patterns, indexes, pagination (keyset), N+1 avoidance, read/write ratio | query-count tests for key endpoints |
| Caching | what, TTL, invalidation, stampede protection | no caching of decision data |
| Concurrency | async I/O end to end, no sync over async, pools sized (Little's law) | pool sizing documented |
| Resilience | timeouts from budgets, retries in one layer, bulkheads, load shedding, fallbacks | timeouts and shedding configured |
| Payloads | DTO sizes, compression, serialisation (source-generated) | size budgets |
| Runtime | GC mode, container CPU and memory, warm-up | no tight CPU limits on hot services |
| Capacity | load test at 1.5x peak with realistic data, soak test, failure test | results reviewed |
| Observability | latency histograms per route, per-stage queue latency, profiling available | dashboards and alerts |
| Growth | data retention, partitioning plan, archive | plan for 3 years |
| Regression | CI budgets (allocations, query counts), canary analysis | in pipeline |
questions.code:
~~~bash
# Pre-go-live performance gate (automated parts)
dotnet test tests/Performance --filter "Category=QueryBudget|Category=AllocationBudget"
k6 run perf/journey-make-payment.js -e RATE=$((PEAK_RPS * 3 / 2)) -e DURATION=30m --summary-export=load.json
jq -e '.metrics.http_req_duration.values["p(99)"] < 1500' load.json
k6 run perf/soak-make-payment.js -e RATE=$PEAK_RPS -e DURATION=6h --summary-export=soak.json
jq -e '.metrics.http_req_failed.values.rate < 0.001' soak.json
kubectl get deploy payments-api -n payments -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources}'   # no tight CPU limits
~~~
pts: Budgets from SLOs; critical path hop counts.
Data access, caching, concurrency, resilience.
Payload sizes and runtime configuration.
Load, soak and failure tests at 1.5x peak.
Observability, growth plans and regression gates.
questions.ex: A design review of a new card-servicing API found six sequential downstream calls on the critical path and OFFSET pagination on transaction history. Fixing both before build cost two days; after launch, the service met its p99 budget at 2x the forecast peak.
fu: Which checks can be automated?
How do you review performance for event-driven services?
What if the forecast is unknown?

cheat:
### Fundamentals
Latency is a distribution: report p50, p95, p99, p99.9 from histograms; averages lie. Fan-out turns component tails into common cases (1 - 0.99^n). Little's law L = arrival rate × time in system; latency multiplies as utilisation approaches 100% (run at 60 to 70%). Method: define, baseline, trace, hypothesise, profile, fix the biggest contributor (Amdahl), verify, prevent regression.

### .NET runtime
Async I/O end to end; no .Result or sync I/O; Task.WhenAll for independent calls; cancellation tokens. Thread pool starvation: queue length up, slow thread injection, low CPU. Lock contention: no I/O under locks, shard state, lock-free snapshots. GC: gen0/1/2, LOH at 85 KB, Server GC, DATAS, heap count and limits; reduce allocations first (Span, ArrayPool, string.Create, SearchValues, FrozenDictionary). Tools: dotnet-counters, dotnet-trace, dotnet-gcdump, dotnet-dump, BenchmarkDotNet, continuous profiling. Startup: ReadyToRun, Native AOT, warm-up before readiness.

### Data access
EF Core: projections, AsNoTracking, split queries, compiled queries, ExecuteUpdate. Keyset pagination with opaque cursors. Pools sized by Little's law; total across replicas within DB limits; HttpClient via factory; one Redis multiplexer. Parameter sniffing: covering indexes, PSP, RECOMPILE for rare heavy queries. Replicas for display reads; decisions on primary; read-your-writes windows. Partition large tables by date, archive by switching, date-bounded queries.

### Caching and I/O
Cache-aside, HybridCache L1+L2 with stampede protection, versioned or event-driven invalidation with version guards, no caching of decision data. Stream files with Pipelines; bounded Channels for stages; batch writes by size and time; source-generated JSON; serialise to streams; compression at the edge.

### Distributed performance
Latency budgets per hop from the SLO; inner timeouts shorter than outer; deadline propagation; hedging for idempotent reads after p95; adaptive concurrency limits and priority load shedding; retry budgets. Reduce chattiness: batch APIs, parallelism, local read models, gRPC internally. Event pipelines: measure queue, processing and relay delays per stage; retry topics; partitions planned for peaks.

### Testing
Open-model load tests (arrival rate), avoid coordinated omission, realistic data, long soaks, ramp past the cliff. Deterministic CI gates (allocations, query counts, bundle sizes), staging comparisons, canary p99 ratios, production shadowing for side-effect-free requests.

### Kubernetes and cost
Avoid tight CPU limits (CFS throttling); requests from measured usage; DOTNET_PROCESSOR_COUNT aligned; HPA fast up, slow down. Unit cost per transaction; efficiency before capacity.

### Principal moves
Journey performance budgets and a paved road; peak readiness programme with vendor quotas and degradation levels; 10x scaling via partitioning, append-only ledgers, async flows and cells; microsecond paths with in-memory single-owner partitions; profile before rewriting; fair decision-grade benchmarks; edge termination and home regions for global latency; communicate in business outcomes with options.
